title: 5 days Upper Lower program review (part. 2)
summary: NH reviews week two of a viewer's 5-day upper/lower-based gentleman split, whose main flaw is greed: too many redundant exercises for the same muscles. He criticizes compound-replicating machines and pulldowns, reshuffles squat and pressing variations across weeks, and advises on hyperextension progression, ab and forearm placement, and rest-day placement.
claims: The program's main flaw is greed: too many unneeded exercises that lengthen sessions, add junk volume and stack the same body part so it cannot return to baseline
The trap bar deadlift is a fine pull from the floor but reduces the hip hinge, so pair it with a more hinge-focused lift; it suits athletes who do not want to invest in deadlift technique
High reps with heavy weights on lower body movements are underrated for hypertrophy; doing low reps for legs and high reps for upper body limits your intensity manipulation
Kettlebell lunges are limited by the heaviest kettlebells available and turn into a grip exercise
Supersetting two different muscles with two different movements is beginner-safe; supersetting the same muscle with the same movement pattern is advanced and usually bad without a clear reason
Pick either seated or standing hamstring curls and push progression on it; he prefers seated
2x20 hyperextensions only make sense if the lower back was pre-fatigued; otherwise do 4x10-15 and progress beyond a 45 lb plate to dumbbells or a barbell
Hyperextensions and hip thrusts are low-specificity lifts; alternate them rather than doing both, even rotating weekly
3 sets of 20-30 standing calf raises is fine for calves
He is biased against machines that replicate compounds: they remove stabilization, lock you into one angle and usually cut the range short at the bottom stretch
Replace lat pulldowns with chin-ups for better results; pulldowns are inferior for hypertrophy, use light ones only as an accessory
Rear delts need little work; the frequency of hitting them is what drives size
Do lying triceps extensions on a bench, not the floor, because the floor removes the stretch
Exercises that need no rest afterwards, like cable rows, should be supersetted or put in a giant set
Alternate weeks between a strength-work week and a small-muscle giant-set week for useful variety
A week without barbell squats risks de-learning the pattern; rotate SSB squat and hack squat across the two weeks instead
Do not overload machines: the need to stabilize free weights is an injury-warning mechanism, and structural integrity fails before the muscle tears
Minimalism suits lower days, but each day still needs at least one barbell compound to justify showing up
Avoid close-grip and football-bar pressing on back-to-back days; repeating triceps-heavy grips turns a shoulder-saving choice into an elbow injury risk
Matching grips across a day can turn weeks into themes, concentrating all of one quality in one week and none in the other
Real dips are probably better than a dip machine
Side raises and rear flies fatigue each other, so supersetting them can reduce performance
Hack squats are good because their angle allows deep range of motion
If using kettlebells, do swings; RDLs are a safe hip hinge you should load heavily, which kettlebells rarely allow
Needing extra hamstring curls after RDLs and hip thrusts means you are not progressing the first two exercises enough
Lower days tax the core most through bracing, so isolated ab work belongs on upper days while fresh; he himself trains abs on lower days
Upper days fry the grip; do forearm work on rest days or lower days (if using straps), and avoid it before upper or deadlift days
As a template's weekly frequency evolves, the position of the rest day should move too
